issues.legal_issue: A tenant’s use of leased premises for a purpose different from the purpose specifically stipulated in the lease is a prohibited change of use that may support eviction.
material_facts: The lease specified that the open land was to be used for sugarcane crushing and the shop connected with that business, and allowed a temporary shed.
The tenant continued to occupy the land and used it to sell cloth and ready-made clothes, asserting that this was permissible during the off-season for the sugarcane business.
The lower courts found that the tenant had used the premises for a purpose different from the one for which they were leased, and the Supreme Court found no reason to disturb those findings.
issues.conclusion: The different use was contrary to the lease purpose and supported eviction under Section 13(1)(a) of the Bombay Rent Act read with Section 108(o) of the Transfer of Property Act; the appeal was dismissed.
issues.legal_principle: Section 13(1)(a) of the Bombay Rent Act makes a tenant liable to eviction for an act contrary to Section 108(o) of the Transfer of Property Act. Section 108(o) requires a lessee not to use or permit use of the leased property for a purpose other than that for which it was leased. The Court relied on the express purpose stipulated in the lease and the concurrent factual findings; it cited no earlier cases.

predicates.tenant_eviction_appeal: The tenant appealed after courts upheld eviction based on alleged use of the leased property for a different purpose.
predicates.lease_specified_a_particular_use: The lease stated a particular purpose for which the tenant could use the property.
predicates.tenant_used_the_property_for_a_different: The tenant used the property to conduct a business different from the one specified in the lease.

issues.definition: When a tenant appeals an eviction based on a different use, a lease specifying a particular use and the tenant’s use of the property for a different business lead to liability for eviction for change of use.

issues.legal_issue: A concurrent finding rejecting a landlord-acquiescence defense to a tenant’s change of use is not disturbed when there is no reason to do so.
material_facts: The tenant argued that the landlord had acquiesced in the different use of the premises.
The trial court and appellate court rejected that plea, and the High Court accepted their finding.
The Supreme Court found no reason to disturb the lower courts’ finding.
issues.conclusion: The tenant’s acquiescence plea did not prevent eviction, and the concurrent finding against that plea was left undisturbed.
issues.legal_principle: The Court applied no separate statutory test or earlier case concerning acquiescence; it accepted the concurrent factual finding against the tenant and stated that there was no reason to disturb it.

predicates.tenant_eviction_appeal: The tenant appealed in proceedings concerning an eviction order.
predicates.lower_courts_rejected_the_acquiescence_p: The lower courts found against the tenant’s claim that the landlord acquiesced in the different use.
predicates.no_reason_to_disturb_the_concurrent_find: The Supreme Court found no reason to set aside the lower courts’ concurrent finding.

issues.definition: In a tenant’s eviction appeal, when the lower courts reject the claim of landlord acquiescence and there is no reason to disturb that finding, the tenant cannot rely on acquiescence to defeat eviction.
